name: Battle of the Granicus
info: In May 334 BCE Alexander the Great of Macedon defeated the field army of the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the crossing of the Granicus in the Troad, the first of his three major battles with the Achaemenid Empire.

facts.date: May 334 BCE, in the Macedonian month of Daisios
facts.place: The crossing of the Granicus (now the Biga River) in the Troad, on the road from Abydus to Dascylium, in north-western Turkey; the exact ford is debated
facts.sides: Macedon under Alexander III, with 12,000 heavy infantry, 1,000 light infantry and 5,100 cavalry, 18,100 men in all; the Persian satraps of Asia Minor, with Arsites probably in overall command, and Memnon of Rhodes, with strengths that range from 14,000 or 15,000 in one modern estimate to almost 20,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry in Arrian
facts.outcome: Alexander defeated the Persian field army and the Greek mercenaries behind it. The Persians were forced onto the defensive in the cities they still held in the region.

t: Strengths for the Persian army run from 14,000 or 15,000 in one modern estimate to Arrian's almost 20,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry, and Justin's 600,000 is judged fantastical.
The ancient accounts disagree about how the battle began: Arrian and Plutarch describe an assault across a defended river, Diodorus a crossing at dawn that met no resistance.
The Persian army was not destroyed, and many of its men retreated to Halicarnassus, but Sardis fell and Alexander marched on to Halicarnassus without significant obstacles.
dyk: Before the battle some Macedonian officers objected that custom forbade fighting in the month of Daisios, and Alexander is said to have solved this by declaring the month a second Artemision.
ev: Philip II wins at Chaeronea and forms the Hellenic League to make war on Persia, while Artaxerxes III is murdered
A Macedonian expeditionary corps lands in Asia Minor, Philip is murdered and Alexander III and Darius III take their thrones
Memnon of Rhodes defeats a Macedonian force and most Greek cities return to Persian control
Alexander marches to the Hellespont and crosses into Asia Minor
Alexander defeats the Persian satraps' army at the Granicus
Dascylium, Sardis and Ephesus fall to Alexander or are evacuated by their garrisons
Alexander besieges Miletus, which resists him

sections.background:
After winning the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, King Philip II of Macedon forced most of the Greek states into a military alliance, the Hellenic League. Its goal was to make war on the Persian Achaemenid Empire to avenge the second Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. The empire had been in crisis since the murder of its king, Artaxerxes III, in 338 BCE, and Egypt again seceded. In the spring of 336 BCE Philip ordered a Macedonian expeditionary corps of several thousand soldiers to land on the western coast of Asia Minor, most likely under Parmenion, with Attalus as second in command. Many Greek cities there surrendered peacefully.

At the end of 336 BCE this changed. Philip was murdered, most likely in October, and his son Alexander III first had to put down revolts in the Balkans and Greece. Darius III had become Great King around the autumn of 336 BCE, stabilised the empire and started a counteroffensive. After the Egyptian revolt was suppressed, he sent Memnon of Rhodes to Asia Minor with a force of Greek mercenaries. Memnon defeated a Macedonian force at either Magnesia ad Sipylum or Magnesia on the Maeander, probably in early spring 335 BCE. Later that year another Macedonian force was defeated by a Persian army in the Troad. By the end of 335 BCE most of the Greek cities were again under Persian control, and the expeditionary force held only Abydus and perhaps Rhoeteum.

Alexander marched his army to the Hellespont in early spring 334 BCE. Darius had probably been informed of his movements for some time, but left the defence of Asia Minor to his satraps.
sections.forces:
Alexander's army that crossed the Hellespont numbered around 32,000 infantry and around 5,000 cavalry, but the Greek allied and mercenary infantry were not used in the battle. The force that fought had 12,000 heavy infantry, including the Foot Companions and the elite hypaspists, 1,000 light infantry of archers and Agrianian javelin-men, and 5,100 cavalry, which makes 18,100 men. Alexander commanded the right wing, where he placed seven of his eight squadrons of Companion cavalry. Parmenion commanded the left, with the Thracian, allied Greek and Thessalian cavalry.

For the Persians Arrian gives almost 20,000 infantry, all Greek mercenaries, and 20,000 cavalry. Diodorus gives 10,000 cavalry and 100,000 infantry, and Justin 600,000 men in all. Azar Gat holds that Greek sources wildly exaggerated the size of Persian armies. N. G. L. Hammond accepts Arrian's numbers, while A. M. Devine and Krzysztof Nawotka call Justin's and Diodorus's infantry figures fantastical. Devine suggests an army of 14,000 to 15,000, with 4,000 or 5,000 Greek mercenaries, and Nawotka and Ernst Badian think part of the infantry was local levies.

The army was led by satraps and commanders including Arsites, Spithridates, Arsames, Rheomithres and Memnon, with Arsites probably in overall command. At a council at Zeleia, Arrian and Diodorus say Memnon advised a scorched earth strategy, but the others refused. The Persians placed their cavalry along the river bank, and the Greek mercenaries, led by Omares, stood behind them. When they saw Alexander opposite their left wing, they moved cavalry there.
sections.course:
Arrian reports that when Alexander learned where the Persians stood, he formed his army for battle. Parmenion advised camping on the west bank and crossing at dawn, but Alexander ordered an immediate attack. Alexander sent Amyntas, son of Arrhabaeus, against the Persian left wing, with the Companion squadron of Socrates, now led by Ptolemy, son of Philip, in front. The Persians answered with javelin volleys. Amyntas's force, outnumbered and below the Persians on the bank, suffered losses and fell back towards Alexander, who then attacked with the rest of the right-wing Companion cavalry.

Devine reads the first attack as a ruse to draw the Persian cavalry out of formation into the riverbed. How Alexander crossed is disputed. Fuller and Bosworth have him moving diagonally downstream towards the Persian centre. Badian has him attacking the massed left wing, and Hammond has him moving upstream to keep his line as it crossed.

In the hard fighting the Macedonian lance proved more effective than the Persian javelin. Alexander broke his lance, and Demaratus of Corinth gave him another. He killed Mithridates, son-in-law of Darius. Cleitus the Black cut off the sword arm of Spithridates as he was about to strike Alexander from behind. The Persian left and then the centre were broken, and the Persian cavalry on both wings fled. Alexander did not pursue far but turned on the Greek mercenaries, who had mostly stayed at their position. They were attacked by the Foot Companions from the front and the cavalry from all other directions, and only a few escaped.
sections.aftermath:
Macedonian losses, in Arrian, were 25 Companion cavalry in the first attack, 60 other cavalry and 30 infantry, 115 killed in all. Plutarch gives 34 dead and Justin 9 infantry and 120 cavalry. On the Persian side many leaders died, among them Niphates, Petenes, Mithrobuzanes, the satrap of Cappadocia, Arbupales, Pharnaces and Omares. Arsites fled into Phrygia and later committed suicide, blamed for the defeat. Arrian states that 1,000 Persian cavalry were killed and 2,000 Greek mercenaries taken prisoner. Plutarch gives 2,500 cavalry and 20,000 infantry killed, and Diodorus 2,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry killed and 20,000 prisoners. Devine, who judges the last two impossibly large, puts the total Persian loss at 5,000 to 6,000.

The 2,000 captured mercenaries were sent to Macedon to work the land as slaves, because Alexander held that they had betrayed fellow Greeks and broken the Hellenic League's agreement. He sent 300 suits of Persian armour to Athens as an offering to Athena. Dascylium was evacuated and occupied by Parmenion, Sardis surrendered, and Ephesus was evacuated by its garrison of Greek mercenaries. Magnesia and Tralles offered surrender. Alexander sent Lysimachus to the cities of Aeolis and Ionia to break up oligarchies and reinstate democratic government. Miletus resisted, and he besieged it.

A large part of the Persian army retreated to Halicarnassus.
sections.sources:
Three ancient accounts survive, by Arrian, Plutarch and Diodorus Siculus. Arrian's is the longest and most detailed. Plutarch's is shorter, concentrates on Alexander's combats with the Persian leaders, and agrees with Arrian except in small points: it puts Persian infantry as well as cavalry in the front line and has the Foot Companions cross the river while the cavalry fought. Diodorus differs fundamentally: the armies camp on opposite banks, and Alexander crosses unopposed at dawn the next day. Most historians dismiss it, since a night or dawn crossing would probably have been detected and opposed, and Diodorus's separate cavalry and infantry battle is uncharacteristic of the Macedonians.

Devine notes that Arrian's casualty figures come from Ptolemy I, who drew on Callisthenes, and that Plutarch's come from Aristobulus. Arrian's order of events may have made Alexander look more heroic, and the debates with Parmenion may come from Callisthenes. Peter Green, in 1974, tried to reconcile Diodorus and Arrian by supposing a failed first crossing against infantry that Alexander's propagandists later covered up, but in 2013 he conceded that the theory was not convincing.

The site is also disputed. The ford has traditionally been placed above the junction of the Gümüşçay river and the Biga River, or further downstream. Hammond placed it between Gümüşçay and Çeşmealtı, where there was a ridge for the mercenaries and perhaps an older riverbed. Modern observers find the river easy to cross, against the ancient writers' emphasis on hardship.
sections.legacy:
The battle was the first of three major battles between Alexander and the Achaemenid Empire. The Persian military losses were not disastrous, but the strategic outcome was precarious for the empire. Satraps had been defeated in Asia Minor before and Sardis had been besieged, but this was the first time the citadel of Sardis had fallen and an enemy force could march on to Halicarnassus without significant obstacles. The Persians were forced onto the defensive in the cities they still held.

Alexander commemorated the victory. The inscription over the armour sent to Athens read, "Alexander, son of Philip and all the Greeks except the Lacedaemonians, present this offering from the spoils taken from the barbarians inhabiting Asia", which marked the absence of the Spartans from his united Greek army. At Dion, in the sanctuary of Zeus, he erected the Granicus Monument, bronze statues by Lysippus of himself and the twenty-five companions who had died in the first cavalry charge, all on horseback. In 146 BCE, after the Fourth Macedonian War, Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus took the group to Rome, where it was displayed in a portico he built below the Capitoline Hill.

The site of the battle has recently been made a protected historic site in Turkey.

summary: In May 334 BCE Alexander the Great defeated the army of the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the crossing of the Granicus. The Persian losses are put at 5,000 to 6,000 by one modern estimate, and the satraps were left on the defensive as Sardis and other cities fell.

notes: Persian strength: Arrian, Diodorus and Justin give wildly different totals; modern views listed in the article, not chosen between. Persian loss of 5,000 to 6,000 is Devine's reasoning only; the summary says so.
Article's lead says Alexander 'defeated the field army of the Persian satraps'; the Aftermath section says the losses were 'not disastrous', so I avoided 'destroyed'.
Spithridates appears also as Sphithridates in the article; I used Spithridates throughout. Arrian's 'Arrhabeus' and 'Arrhabaeus' both appear; used Arrhabaeus.
The ev entry for 334 BCE on Dascylium, Sardis and Ephesus is undated within the year in the article.
The article gives the Macedonian force as 18,100 for the battle and around 32,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry for the army that crossed: both given, not reconciled.

Left out: the detail of each unit's commander in the Macedonian line, Aretis's broken lance, the sun-in-the-eyes argument against Diodorus, the criticism of Persian deployments and Atizyes (Diodorus lists him as killed here and at Issus).
